title: Amazon is buying billions in Nvidia AI systems it can't yet turn on
content:
Amazon is racing to secure AI hardware earlier than before, even as data center power shortages leave some GPU systems waiting in warehouses.
Under a new Early Rack Receipt process, AWS expected to receive roughly $5 billion in Nvidia's GB300 server racks at US facilities before final deployment, according to August internal emails reviewed by Business Insider. The company projected roughly $3 billion more in GB300 racks each month "for the foreseeable future," one of the emails said.
Some AWS sites had room for more racks but not enough available power to turn them on, people familiar with the effort said, leaving finished equipment to be staged at intermediary warehouses until the facilities were ready.
At least one AWS team did not have "a clear forecasted path" for getting the incoming racks into data centers at the time, according to one of the emails.
Dark GPUs
A lack of new electricity capacity is one of several bottlenecks slowing the buildout of some AI data centers. This has led to a phenomenon known as dark GPUs, where AI chips and servers are purchased but can sit idle due to power supply issues or other challenges. (Dark GPUs can also refer to system design flaws that mean this gear isn't fully used after being plugged in).
This is partly why financial pressure is mounting on big data center projects. Money must be spent upfront to secure supplies of Nvidia GPUs and other valuable AI components. But if some data centers aren't ready to run, those early investments can tie up huge amounts of cash. Debt financing can fill in the gaps, but the market has become less willing to lend against some of these projects lately.
Trade-off
Amazon's early-rack program is one piece of the cloud leader's broader AI buildout, which is putting new pressure on its cash flow, as Business Insider exclusively reported this week. Amazon expects roughly $220 billion in capital expenditures this year — more than any Big Tech peer. Its free-cash-flow turned negative last quarter for the first time since 2023, and could stay negative for a while.
For AWS, the trade-off is securing scarce GPU racks before competitors do, even if some data centers are not yet ready to turn them on. But taking ownership earlier can tie up billions in equipment before it starts generating cloud revenue.
Previously, AWS took ownership of a finished rack only upon delivery to a data center, according to internal documents. Under the new approach, it can pay for and record certain racks earlier in the supply chain.
An Amazon spokesperson said the company routinely stages finished hardware near deployment sites so it can install it once capacity becomes available, calling the practice "best business practice." The spokesperson added that Amazon has long-established systems for tracking infrastructure assets and disputed that the broader company lacked a path for getting racks into data centers.
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy previously said the company has a "clear line of sight" to strong returns from its AI investments, calling the technology a "once in a lifetime opportunity."
"We've been through this cycle with the first big AWS growth wave, and liked the results," Jassy wrote in Amazon's annual shareholder letter. "We expect to feel similarly about this next wave."

report.summary: Amazon is securing billions in Nvidia GB300 racks early, but power shortages mean some systems sit in warehouses—tying up cash before they generate revenue.
report.background: The AI boom has shifted data-center construction into a race for scarce GPUs, servers, land, and electricity. Cloud providers are committing enormous capital upfront to lock in Nvidia systems before competitors, betting that AI demand will justify the spend. But new electricity capacity, grid connections, and facility readiness often lag hardware delivery. That mismatch has produced 'dark GPUs': expensive AI equipment that is purchased but cannot be fully powered or used. Amazon's early-rack program is part of a broader buildout that is straining its cash flow, as capital expenditures reach record levels and free cash flow turns negative. The episode illustrates a wider industry tension: AI compute is becoming available faster than the power infrastructure needed to run it, forcing cloud providers into financial and logistical trade-offs.
key_points: Under AWS's new Early Rack Receipt process, Amazon expected to receive about $5 billion in Nvidia GB300 server racks at US facilities before final deployment, according to internal emails. One email projected roughly $3 billion more in GB300 racks each month 'for the foreseeable future.' Previously, AWS took ownership only when a finished rack reached a data center.

Some AWS sites had space for additional racks but lacked available power to turn them on, so finished equipment was staged in intermediary warehouses. At least one AWS team lacked 'a clear forecasted path' for moving incoming racks into data centers, an email said. This is the 'dark GPUs' problem: expensive AI hardware bought but idle because power or facilities are not ready.

The strategy creates a financial squeeze. Amazon must pay for scarce Nvidia systems upfront, but the equipment cannot generate cloud revenue until installed and powered. Amazon expects about $220 billion in capital expenditures this year, more than Big Tech peers, and free cash flow turned negative last quarter. Debt financing can bridge gaps, but lenders have become less willing to fund some data-center projects.

AWS is trading financial flexibility for supply security, taking ownership earlier to beat competitors to scarce GPU racks. Amazon says staging hardware near deployment sites is 'best business practice,' disputes that it lacks a path to install racks, and says it has long-standing asset-tracking systems. CEO Andy Jassy calls AI a 'once in a lifetime opportunity' and expects returns similar to AWS's first growth wave.
report.impact: The story highlights that power, not chip supply alone, is becoming the binding constraint on AI buildouts. For the industry, early rack purchases may become standard as cloud providers race to lock in Nvidia capacity, but that raises cash-flow and financing risks and could increase the number of 'dark GPUs' sitting idle. For developers, GPU capacity may arrive unevenly: some regions could face delays or higher prices even as hardware is bought, making utilization monitoring and power-aware scheduling more important. For regular users, the practical effect is slower-than-expected expansion of AI services and continued pressure on cloud and AI pricing; the compute is being secured, but the electricity and facilities needed to use it are lagging.
report.tools: Readers tracking this infrastructure bottleneck can explore Nvidia DCGM for GPU health and utilization telemetry, Prometheus and Grafana for dashboards, Kubernetes device plugins and Ray or Slurm for scheduling AI workloads, and OpenDCIM or NetBox for data-center capacity and power documentation. These open-source and freemium tools help teams spot idle 'dark GPUs,' plan power-aware deployments, and improve utilization before buying more hardware.
